headline: Games Built for Those Who Survived: How Transplant Athletes Find Hope
meta_description: 600 organ transplant recipients gathered in the Netherlands for the European Transplant Games, discovering that competition matters far less than belonging.
summary_short: At the European Transplant Games in Arnhem, organ recipients compete not for glory but for something deeper: proof that life after transplant can be full and active.
body:
When Robert Lindemann, a 32-year-old accountant, travelled to Arnhem in June as one of 600 athletes competing in the European Transplant Games, he found something unexpected: relief. Eight months after his heart transplant, he was no longer the only one in the room living with a new organ. The week-long event—open to transplant recipients, living donors, family members, and people undergoing dialysis—created a space where his extraordinary medical history felt ordinary. "Everybody has a special story," he says. But the real power wasn't in competition; it was in witnessing transplant recipients who had passed the median 14 to 15-year post-transplant survival mark and were still active, proving another life was possible.

Edelle Collins, now 50, arrived apprehensive. After a double lung transplant in 2021 followed by kidney problems requiring dialysis three times a week, she struggled to imagine improvement. Yet after earning a bronze medal in darts and surviving an intense heatwave, she felt something shift. "I feel definitely more motivated now," she said. What surprised her most wasn't the competition—it was belonging to a group where "no explanation is needed" about her past. "Nobody's really interested in your big, long sob story," she reflected, "because we all have sob stories."

These games, first held in Portsmouth in 1978, have evolved into a biannual global event reflecting a profound shift in transplant medicine. Modern surgery, immunosuppression medications, and better follow-up care mean recipients can now do activities once considered impossible. For many, the emotional weight of waiting and recovery makes these gathering spaces invaluable—places where hope isn't abstract, but embodied in the athletes around them.
